With advancements in lens technology and impressive lumens per watt, Greenhse Technologies Area Lights are designed to illuminate vast spaces effectively, even when mounted at lower heights. These lights offer reliable performance with minimal energy consumption, whether for industrial yards, sports stadiums or parking lots. This guide explains what an area light is, where it is used, the features of the Greenhse GH-A200, GH-A300 and GH-A500 range, and the popular models available in Perth.

What is an area or street light?

An area light emits light from a defined surface rather than a single point like a spotlight. The resulting light creates soft shadows and a more realistic lighting effect, which minimises harsh shadows and produces even lighting across the ground.

Area lights are used where high-powered lighting is required: sports stadiums, parking lots, tennis courts and similar spaces. The lights have adjustable beam angles to cover different parts of a field. They provide high brightness in lumens with lower power consumption, are extremely energy-efficient and have long lifespans. Anti-glare optics prevent blinding players and spectators, which is a common problem with older floodlights.

Uses of LED area lights

LED area lights are versatile and suit both outdoor and indoor applications. Key use cases include:

  • Sports facilities
  • Parking lots
  • Industrial yards and warehouses
  • Commercial and hospitality venues

GH-A200 / GH-A300 / GH-A500: the Greenhse area light range

The Greenhse new area light can be adjusted and set to provide the most suitable lighting solution for a particular application.

Using the correct optical lens, an LED area light can cover up to 3 times the area of a similar-sized traditional LED floodlight, with one third of the power consumption. Optical lenses let the light cover wide areas even at low mounting heights. Wasted spill light is eliminated, which makes the area light more comfortable to be under, safer in traffic areas and more efficient, because every lumen lands where it is needed.

Key adjustable features:

  • CCT colour selectable switch: choose the ideal colour temperature, from 3000K warm white for hotels and hospitality venues to 5000K for industrial yards and warehouses. CCT (correlated colour temperature) describes how warm or cool white light appears; lower numbers are warmer.
  • 1-10V dimmable: the light can be dimmed through a standard 1-10V control circuit.
  • Built-in power selectable switch: set the wattage at installation for quick, low-cost brightness settings without changing fittings.

Combined with diecast alloy housing, the heat sink provides a long lifespan in outdoor settings, with more than 50,000 hours of operation and a 5-year warranty. Good heat management is what keeps LED output stable over the years, so the housing design matters as much as the chips.

Benefits of LED area lights

  • High efficiency, low power: area lights can cover up to three times the area of standard floodlights with the same power.
  • Wide coverage: the same three-times advantage means fewer poles and fewer fittings for a given site.
  • Special lens options: designed to minimise wasted light spillage.
  • Lens options:
    • T2: 150º x 45º
    • T3: 140º x 70º
    • T4: 120º x 90º
    • T5: 90º x 90º
  • T2 lens: perfect for wide-spread lighting, effective even at just 3m mounting height.
  • T5 lens: ideal for longer-distance illumination, such as throwing light across a yard from a tall pole.
  • Smart features: built-in Photo-Lux sensors, interchangeable lenses, colour and power selection options.
  • Dimmable: adjust brightness to suit your needs.
  • Longevity: a very long lifespan of over 50,000 hours.
  • Flexible mounting: various options are available for every situation, including pole, wall and bracket mounts.

Popular LED area light products in Perth

185W LED Street and Area Light

Features:

  • No mercury
  • 5-year warranty
  • IP66 weatherproof, sealed against dust and powerful water jets
  • Lifespan: 120,000 h
  • Replaces: 400w metal halide

300W LED Area Light

Features:

  • Low heat output
  • 5-year warranty
  • Lifespan: 120,000 hrs
  • Replaces 1000w metal halide
  • Weight: 8.6 / 8.9 kg nett/gross

Both models are 5000K, suited to car parks, yards and sports areas where crisp white light aids visibility. Because they replace 400w and 1000w metal halide lamps with far lower wattage, the energy saving on a site that runs lights all night is substantial. Installation and pole wiring must be completed by a licensed electrician.

Greenhse Technologies combines cutting-edge design with energy-efficient performance to offer the best lighting solutions. Adequate lighting is essential for safety, efficiency and performance in every environment, and we aim to provide unmatched efficiency, durability and flexibility, making our area lights the ideal choice for industrial, commercial and outdoor spaces.

/blog/high-bay-led-lights-energy-savings.bodyHtml:
When it comes to upgrading industrial and commercial lighting, Greenhse Technologies is Perth's trusted leader in High Bay LED lights. Our LED lighting solutions are suitable for businesses, warehouses and factories, delivering high brightness, robust performance and remarkable energy efficiency. In this article you will learn about high bay light features, the types we stock, why driver quality matters so much at height, and how to choose the right beam angle for your ceiling.

Why choose High Bay LED lights for your industrial space?

LED high bay lights can offer savings of up to 80% compared to older metal halide or other older lighting options. Greenhse high bays ensure high energy savings while also optimising the light for different applications and ceiling heights.

Utilising specially designed lenses, Greenhse high bays are a lot more effective than a bare LED panel. A narrow lens on a high ceiling pushes light down to the floor where it is needed, while a wide lens on a lower ceiling spreads it evenly between the racks. High lumens per watt also increase efficiency, as the same light output can be achieved with less power consumption. The beam angle diagram shows how the 60º, 90º and 120º lenses relate to mounting height.

Quality and lifespan

Efficiency and effectiveness are important when selecting a high bay, but quality and lifespan are just as important. Greenhse high bay lights can last over 50 000hrs even in harsh environments. Several elements are critical to a long life: housing design, driver and LED chips.

Greenhse high bay lights now utilise Sosen drivers, which after 13 years of testing have proved to be more reliable than any other driver. Since moving to these drivers there has not been a single failure in over 6 years. Good quality LED chips with high LSM 70 values and well-designed aluminium alloy housings provide a good heatsink with effective cooling, and heat is the main enemy of LED life.

Long lifespans are not only important for ensuring a good return on investment. They are critical in eliminating frequent lamp changes, which are very expensive because of the height at which a high bay is installed. Every failure means a scissor lift or boom, downtime on the floor and labour costs that quickly outweigh any saving on a cheaper fitting.

A note on cheaper DOB high bays

Cheaper high bay options may utilise DOB, or driver on board, where the driver circuitry sits on the same board as the LEDs. These provide lower lumens per watt, much shorter lifespans, and have a flicker frequency that could affect working with certain rotating machinery. They are also more sensitive to power surges and failure. The prices are attractive, however, and DOB fittings can be suitable for home sheds or areas that are not used as often.

Greenhse high bay light features

  • Reliable Sosen drivers
  • Frequency free (no flicker)
  • High lumens per watt, above 160
  • Specially designed lenses: 120º, 90º and 60º
  • IP65 weather resistant, so dust and water jets are kept out of the housing
  • Long lifespan of over 50 000hrs
  • 5 year warranty
  • Optional CCT switch: 3000K, 4000K or 5000K
  • Optional power selectable: 100%, 75% or 50%
  • Optional smart control

The CCT switch lets the installer set the colour temperature on site, from warm 3000K through neutral 4000K to cool 5000K, which most warehouses and workshops prefer for visibility. The power selector allows the same fitting to be set to 75% or 50% output in lower areas or where fewer lumens are needed, saving energy without changing the product.

Comprehensive LED lighting solutions in Perth

At Greenhse Technologies, our range of high bay LED lights is tailored to meet the diverse needs of industrial and commercial clients in Perth. Our key products include:

  • 100W LED high bay light with 120º beam, suited to lower ceilings and general areas.

  • 200W LED high bay light with 120º beam, for large open floor areas.
  • 200W LED high bay light with 90º beam, for higher ceilings and aisles between racking.

We also offer cost-effective bulk purchasing plans and Australia-wide shipping, ensuring maximum value and convenience for larger fit-outs. High bay lights operate on 240V and must be installed by a licensed electrician.

High bay LED lights are powerful fixtures designed for spaces with high ceilings, typically 6 metres or more. Warehouses, factories, gymnasiums and large retail floors need this type of lighting to deliver consistent brightness across a wide floor area.

Traditional warehouse lighting relied on metal halide lamps, fluorescent tube systems and high-pressure sodium lights. These older systems consume a lot of energy, need frequent maintenance and produce uneven light output. By comparison, warehouse high bay lights built on LED technology provide:

/blog/high-voltage-240v-strip-lighting.h.bodyHtml:
Professional 240V continuous lighting is the simplest way to light a long ceiling recess, bulkhead or building outline in one unbroken run. GH 240V Strip Lighting from Greenhse Technologies is fully certified to Australian Standards, the only 240V LED strip light with this certification in Australia. This post explains how high voltage strip lighting differs from low voltage strip, why it is so easy to install, how it is ordered and dimmed, and how to place it in a recess so the ceiling lights evenly.

Why 240V strip beats low voltage strip for long runs

Low voltage strip runs on 12V or 24V, so every run needs a transformer (LED driver). Voltage drop limits each run to about 5 metres, which means a long bulkhead needs multiple transformers, multiple controllers, aluminium channels and long wiring between them. The result is expensive, time-consuming to install, prone to uneven lighting where runs meet, and less reliable, with more parts that can fail and a shorter life span.

GH 240V strip lighting has numerous advantages over low voltage strip. It is very strong, bright and has good LED density, but the biggest advantage is its strength and being very easy to install. A single strip can be up to 30 metres long. All that is required is a plug in the recess connected to a wall switch. No transformers, no joins, no wires, just one plug. The strip is plug and play, installs within minutes and lasts for decades.

Made to size, plug and play

Strip lights are made to size, to the closest metre, with a factory-fitted AC adapter and plug. Ordering is straightforward:

  1. Measure the total distance of the run around the ceiling or bulkhead (distance A on a plan view, starting from the power point).
  2. Round up to the closest metre.
  3. The strip gets made to that size and arrives ready to plug in.

Because the strip carries mains voltage, the power point in the recess and the wall switch must be installed by a licensed electrician. Fixing the strip in place and plugging it in is the easy part.

Dimming, colour and LED density

The strip is dimmable with Triac wall switch dimmers, the same leading-edge or trailing-edge dimmers used for other 240V lighting, so no separate dimming controller is needed. It is available in a number of colour choices, from warm to cool white.

With up to 180 LEDs per metre and high quality LED chips, the strip produces bright, seamless lit ceilings with no visible dots or dark patches. That quality makes it suitable for hotels, shopping centres and high quality homes where a continuous line of light is part of the architecture.

Full colour 240V strip light is also available. It requires an RGB controller, which can work with a selection of colour remotes or with your smart device. Add an optional gateway and the strip can be controlled by voice through Google or Alexa, which is popular for feature ceilings, alfresco areas and festive outlines on the front of a house.

How to place strip in a recess for even light

Where the strip sits inside the recess decides how the light washes across the ceiling. The guide below covers the two most common recess sizes.

Recess around 150 mm wide by 50 mm high

  • Wrap the strip around the bulkhead on the back edge (A) of the recess, facing inwards towards the room.
  • Do not fix it on the front edge (B). Light from the front edge cannot reach across the ceiling.
  • Placed sideways on the back edge, the strip supplies even lighting across the whole ceiling.

Recess around 100 mm wide by 100 mm high

  • A deep, narrow recess with the strip mounted flat on the floor of the recess will only light the corner, leaving the ceiling beyond it dark. This is the incorrect placement.
  • The solution is to raise the internal height. Install a profile inside the recess to lift the strip closer to the top, then mount the strip on it facing the room. Light then travels out across the ceiling evenly.

Fix the strip with special Permastick mounting tape, available from Bunnings. This double-sided acrylic tape has high bond strength, heat resistance and maximum weather resistance, so it holds the strip on a bulkhead for the long term.

Where 240V strip lighting works best

  • Continuous ceiling recesses and bulkheads in living areas, kitchens and hallways.
  • Hotel corridors, lobbies and shopping centre ceilings where runs are long and reliability matters.
  • Outdoor eaves, alfresco areas and building outlines, particularly in full colour RGB.
  • Any project where a low voltage system would need several transformers and joins.

Talk to Greenhse Technologies in Perth

If you are planning a lit ceiling or bulkhead, bring your measurements to Greenhse Technologies and we can size a certified GH 240V strip to the closest metre, advise on dimming and colour, and show you the placement that gives even light. Visit the showroom at 5/1 Locke Lane, Ellenbrook WA 6069 or phone (08) 9297 2969.

In recent years, the importance of sustainable living has gained significant attention. From reducing carbon footprints to conserving energy, individuals are actively seeking ways to create a more sustainable lifestyle, and the home is one of the easiest places to start. This post explains how LED lights and DC fans can play a crucial role in creating a sustainable home, from lower electricity bills and longer product life to safer materials and smarter control.

LED downlights cut electricity use by 50 to 80%

LED downlights have been a great innovation. They save between 50 and 80% on electricity costs compared with older incandescent, halogen and even fluorescent or compact fluorescent globes. An LED converts most of its power into light rather than heat, which is why a downlight of around 8W to 10W can replace a 50W halogen. That significant reduction in energy consumption translates into lower electricity bills and less strain on the environment. To learn more, read Why LED Downlights are Beneficial.

Better light, not just cheaper light

LED design improvements have also delivered better lighting solutions. Colour temperature can now be selected to suit the room, from warm white for bedrooms and living areas to cool white for kitchens and garages, and many downlights let you switch between settings at installation. New lens designs ensure low glare, so the light is comfortable to sit under rather than a bright spot on the ceiling.

LED lights can also be integrated with smart home systems, enabling homeowners to control and automate their lighting. Smart Bluetooth and WiFi lighting systems allow personalised settings, timers and motion sensors, which optimise energy usage and reduce unnecessary lighting. A hallway light that switches off after two minutes, or a scene that dims the living room at 9pm, saves energy without anyone having to think about it.

Long life means less waste

LED lights have an impressive lifespan, lasting up to 25 times longer than traditional bulbs. This longevity reduces the frequency of replacements and minimises the amount of waste going to landfill. Fewer globes manufactured, packaged, shipped and thrown away is a real sustainability gain in its own right. By choosing LED Downlights, homeowners contribute to a more sustainable waste management system.

Lower carbon footprint, safer materials

The energy efficiency of LED downlights directly translates to a reduced carbon footprint. By using less electricity, LED lights help decrease greenhouse gas emissions from power generation. As more households transition to LED lighting, the collective impact on the environment becomes substantial.

Unlike traditional bulbs, LED lights do not contain toxic materials such as mercury, which makes them safer for both people and the environment at the end of their life. LED lights also generate far less heat, reducing the risk of fire hazards in ceilings and around insulation. The absence of toxic materials and the lower heat output contribute to a healthier and safer living environment.

DC fans: the other half of a sustainable home

Ceiling fans now come with LED lights too, but to maximise energy savings, DC fans are far better than AC fans. A DC fan uses less energy when the speed is reduced, unlike an AC fan, which always draws close to the maximum wattage specified. For example, a DC fan on speed 1 can produce 5 CBM (cubic metres) of airflow using about 7 Watts of energy. An AC fan will use about 75 Watts, which is 10 times more. Even on maximum speed, a good DC fan will use at least 50% less than an AC fan. Read why DC fans are better than AC fans for the full comparison.

Other advantages of a good DC fan are that it is a lot quieter, because it uses brushless motor technology, it has more speed variations, the airflow direction can be reversed for winter, and everything is controllable via a remote. Remote control also makes installation cheaper and easier, as no wall controller needs to be wired in.

Energy cost matters most in a bedroom, the most common place for a fan, where it will run all night, every night. An air conditioner uses between 1000 and 7000 watts per hour, while a DC fan uses about 7 to 20 watts per hour, so the savings are enormous over a Perth summer.

Choosing a DC fan

  • Choose a fan with well-designed blades, as airflow and low running costs are the most important factors.
  • 3 blade fans should produce up to 10 CBM, 4 blade fans 15 CBM, and 5 blade fans 17 CBM of airflow.
  • If purchasing a fan with a light, about 24 watts will be sufficient for a bedroom.

A brighter, more sustainable future

LED lighting has emerged as a popular sustainable solution for modern homes in Perth. LED lights reduce energy consumption and lower electricity bills, and they also contribute to a reduced carbon footprint and a healthier living environment. With their longevity, versatility and smart integration, LED lights give homeowners the opportunity to create a sustainable and efficient home without sacrificing design and functionality. Pair them with a DC fan and the biggest everyday loads in the home, lighting and cooling, are both under control.

Greenhse Technologies aims to provide eco-friendly, energy-efficient LED lighting solutions that create sustainable environments, and is committed to driving positive change through innovative LED lighting. How smart lighting works

Sensors and automation

/blog/how-to-change-5ghz-to-24ghz-to-con.lede: Smart devices are set to work on the 2.4GHz frequency and will not connect on 5GHz. Here is how to switch your WiFi so they pair first time.
/blog/how-to-change-5ghz-to-24ghz-to-con.bodyHtml:
Smart devices such as Kinetic RF switches, smart downlights, smart plugs and WiFi controllers are set to work on the 2.4 GHz WiFi frequency and will not connect or work on 5GHz. This guide explains why that is, how to tell the two bands apart on your router, and how to change your network settings so your smart devices link first time.

Even though 2.4 GHz carries less information than 5 GHz, it has better range and passes through walls and ceilings more easily, which is why smart lighting manufacturers build their products around it. The problem is that many newer routers come with simultaneous 5 GHz and 2.4 GHz bands, called a dual band router. The 5GHz band is quicker, so your phone prefers it and tries to link the smart device through it, which prevents the device from connecting.

Why the linking process needs 2.4 GHz

To enable linking, a separate 2.4 GHz band is required, or the 5 GHz band needs to be temporarily turned off while linking. During the linking process, both your mobile device and your smart device need to be connected to the same 2.4 GHz signal. Once the smart device has joined the network, your phone can go back to 5 GHz for everyday use; the smart device will stay on 2.4 GHz on its own.

You do not need to disable the 5GHz band if you can separate the two bands by logging on to your router and changing the name (SSID) of each band in the settings, for example "my network 2.4" and "my network 5". Then connect your phone to the WiFi name allocated to the 2.4GHz band and use that same name and password when linking the smart device in the app.

Logging into your router configuration page

Your router has a configuration page where you can change and alter settings, the WiFi name and the password. You can also log in and set up a dedicated 2.4GHz network to differentiate it from the 5GHz network, and set your own name and password for each band. The login information is normally printed on a label on the router.

Every router has an IP address (Internet Protocol address) that can be entered into a web browser's address bar. The most common universal addresses are:

  • 192.168.0.1
  • 192.168.1.1

After you enter one of those two addresses, a username and password box will appear. The default login details should be on the router label. Typically they are:

  • Username: admin
  • Password: blank or admin

Once you are logged in, go to the wireless page and set up your own dedicated 2.4GHz network. Sometimes selecting the 2.4GHz "Guest" network may be necessary, as it has fewer security options and some smart devices link to it more reliably.

Step-by-step: separate the bands and link your device

  1. Find the router label and note the IP address, username and password.
  2. Type the IP address into your browser and log in.
  3. Open the wireless or WiFi settings page.
  4. Give the 2.4GHz band its own name, such as "my network 2.4", and give the 5GHz band a different name, such as "my network 5". Set a password for each.
  5. Save the settings and let the router restart.
  6. On your phone, connect to the 2.4GHz network name.
  7. Open the smart app, add the device and enter the 2.4GHz name and password when prompted.
  8. After linking, reconnect your phone to whichever band you prefer.

Band steering: why it stops smart devices linking

Some WiFi routers have a function called "Band Steering". This can be useful for 5GHz products, because it prioritises 5GHz but switches to 2.4GHz as you move further from the router to maintain a connection. The problem with band steering is that both the 2.4GHz and 5GHz bands share the same name and password, so your phone cannot be forced onto 2.4GHz during linking. To set up different names, band steering will need to be turned off in the router settings.

Too many devices? Consider a WiFi extender

Standard home routers are not designed to handle many devices; often 12 is the maximum on each band. If you exceed that number, you will find devices dropping out and showing as offline in your phone app, especially once you have a house full of smart switches and downlights. WiFi extenders and access points can increase the device count to 300 or more and offer better and quicker WiFi management and range across the whole home.

If you add a WiFi extender, connect it to the router with a data cable link (recommended, as it is far more stable than a wireless backhaul). Use the same name and password on the extender's 2.4GHz and 5GHz networks as you set on the router, then turn off the router's own WiFi. Your smart devices will see the same network name and password and will not need to be reset or re-linked.

Help with smart lighting in Perth

Once your 2.4GHz network is sorted, linking Kinetic RF switches, smart downlights and other Tuya and Smart Life devices is usually a matter of minutes. If a device still refuses to connect, bring it in or call Greenhse Technologies on (08) 9297 2969. The showroom at 5/1 Locke Lane, Ellenbrook WA 6069 has working smart lighting on display and the team can walk you through the router settings and app setup for your home.

When it comes to modern lighting solutions, LED batten lights and LED batten fittings have emerged as the preferred choice for residential, commercial and industrial spaces. These energy-efficient fixtures deliver superior illumination, require low maintenance and offer long-lasting performance. This post explains what LED batten lights are, why Greenhse battens are a strong choice in Perth, where they are used, and how to select the right brightness, colour temperature, size and features for your space.

What are LED batten lights?

LED batten lights are linear light fixtures designed to provide bright and even illumination along their full length. They excel in applications such as garages, kitchens, hallways, offices and retail spaces, and they are the natural replacement for the old fluorescent tube fittings found in many Perth homes and workplaces. Compared to traditional fluorescent lights, LED batten fittings are highly energy-efficient and environmentally friendly. The LEDs and driver are built into the fitting, so there are no tubes or starters to replace. Their slim design and superior light output make them a versatile choice for both residential and commercial use.

Why choose Greenhse LED batten lights in Perth?

  • Energy efficiency: LED batten lights consume significantly less power than traditional lighting options, which can lead to lower electricity bills. They typically use about 50% less energy than fluorescent lights. Greenhse batten lights have a high brightness of up to 5800 Lms.
  • Durability: designed to last, these lights have a lifespan of 50,000 hours, reducing the need for frequent replacements. Unlike traditional tubes, LED fixtures resist shocks and vibrations, making them suitable for garages, workshops and other busy environments.
  • Eco-friendly: LED lighting produces less heat and contains no harmful substances such as mercury, which is found in fluorescent tubes. This makes it a safer choice for the environment and for disposal at the end of life.
  • Versatility: available in various sizes and colour temperatures, LED batten fittings can be tailored to diverse needs. Whether you prefer warm white for a cosy atmosphere or cool white for a more vibrant feel, Greenhse batten lights are colour-switch adjustable, so the installer sets the colour on the fitting itself.
  • Cost-effective: with reduced energy consumption and minimal maintenance costs, LED batten lights offer great value for money. Their longevity means fewer replacements, allowing you to save in the long run.

Check out the Greenhse Tri-Colour LED Batten Fitting for the best deals and installation tips.

Applications of LED batten fittings in Perth

Residential spaces

Brighten your kitchen, garage, laundry or hallway with sleek and efficient batten fittings. These lights are designed to blend into any interior while providing excellent illumination, and a single batten will often replace a pair of tired fluorescent tubes with better light and lower running cost.

Commercial areas

Offices, retail stores and showrooms in Perth benefit from the bright, professional lighting offered by batten lights. Their even light distribution improves visibility and work efficiency, and fittings can be surface mounted or suspended in continuous rows.

Industrial use

Warehouses, factories and workshops require reliable lighting. LED batten fittings are durable and resistant to wear and tear, making them well suited to demanding industrial environments where lights run for long hours.

How to choose the right LED batten fittings

Selecting the right LED batten lights for your space depends on several factors:

  • Brightness: measured in lumens, the brightness of your batten light should correspond with the size and purpose of the space. A garage or workshop needs more lumens per square metre than a hallway. A well-lit area promotes productivity and comfort.
  • Colour temperature: choose between warm white, cool white or daylight tones based on the ambience you want to create. Warm white suits living areas, while cool white and daylight suit kitchens, garages and work areas where clear vision matters. A colour-switchable batten lets you decide after installation.
  • Size: ensure the length of the batten fitting aligns with the dimensions of your room or workspace. A well-proportioned fixture enhances both aesthetics and functionality, and matching the length of an existing fluorescent fitting usually covers old fixing holes.
  • Features: consider additional features like motion sensors, dimming capabilities and waterproof designs for outdoor, carport or specific applications. These features can improve the usability and efficiency of your lighting.

Batten fittings connect to 240V mains and must be installed by a licensed electrician, who will also remove any old fluorescent ballast wiring.

  • Competitive pricing with a 3-year warranty.
  • Expert advice and guidance on selecting the right lighting solution.
  • An easy online shopping experience with reliable delivery throughout Perth and Australia.

With benefits such as energy efficiency, durability and versatility, these lights suit homes, offices and industrial settings. LED downlights are the most common lighting in homes and commercial installations. They cost under $10, with installation from $15 to replace a halogen or $20 to $35 for new installations, yet builders charge up to $150 per fitting installed and often compromise light quality. This guide covers the choices, judging quality, and how to select and position downlights.

How to compare and get better quality downlights

1. Lumens

You pay for lumens, not watts; efficient lights give more lumens per watt. Look for output lumens: packaging often quotes chip lumens, and output is about 15% less, sometimes half.

2. Dimming

Check the light is dimmable; dimmer switches affect the range, and some flicker when low. Dimming sets mood, cuts glare, saves power in proportion (unlike halogen) and extends lifespan.

3. Light colour

Most downlights have a 3-colour switch; cheaper ones do not. Common settings: Warm White (3000k), Natural White (4000-4500k) and Cool White (5000-6000k). Check the Kelvin value: some suppliers call 4000-4500k Cool White and 5000-6000k Daylight or Bright White. Warm White is relaxing and preferred by hotels; Natural White has less yellow and is the most popular home choice; Cool White suits offices, with a trend from 6000k to 5000k, easier on the eyes with less blue light. We recommend LED downlights with 3000k, 4000k and 5000k settings. Smart downlights allow any temperature between 2700k and 5700k.

4. CRI, light quality

Kelvin is an average, so two 3000k, 4000k or 5000k lights can differ, some with green or pink tints. Compare CRI (colour-rendering index): over 80% for homes, over 90 for shops and displays.

5. IC-4 or IC-F

Downlights get hot. All should have IC-4 or IC-F certification; IC-4 is higher, indicating under 0.4mm gap so insects and material cannot enter and add fire risk. Certified lights with built-in drivers can abut insulation, needing no gaps or canisters. Never fit uncertified downlights.

6. Certification and public liability

Downlights must meet Australian wiring regulations. Some certification covers part of the fitting, comes from a non-registered laboratory or is not genuine. If a non-compliant fitting, or one not fitted by a registered electrician, causes a fire, insurers will not pay. Check that supplier and electrician hold public liability insurance.

7. Cords and plugs

Unless in a concrete slab, downlights come with cords and sockets, one plug base per light. Hard-wiring voids IC-4/F certification and makes replacement costlier.

8. IP rating

First digit is dust, second water. Rain areas need IP65; under eaves and wet areas IP54 generally suits (your electrician will verify). Higher ratings also keep insects out.

9. Beam angle

Flat white diffusers spread light almost 180º, reaching the walls so rooms look brighter; without wall light a room looks dark whatever the lumens. They suit walk-in wardrobes or two per bedroom, but many together cause glare and suit fans poorly.

10. Low glare

Cheap wide-beam lights push people to excessive brightness and an office-like feel. Low glare lights are more comfortable, add mood and look nicer.

11. Lifespan and warranty

Good downlights are rated 40 000 hours, the time to fall to 70% brightness; commercial LEDs reach 120 000 hours. Drivers can fail earlier; look for surge protection. Warranties can outlast small online sellers, so choose an established company supplying credible, listed Chinese brands. Some suppliers have had over 50% failures within 6 months.

12. Smart downlights

Smart downlights dim, set colour from 2700k to 5700k, offer full colour, timers, alarms and links to other devices. Check:

  • Colour matches your non-smart downlights.
  • Dimming is suitable and flicker-free.
  • Smart lights have permanent memory, or switching scrambles settings.
  • WiFi or Bluetooth: many WiFi lights strain bandwidth; Bluetooth with a cheap gateway avoids this.
  • For RGB, check colour brightness, not just white.
  • Lights are not smart if the switch is off, so change switch and light together. Smart dimmable switches are not yet available.
  • More electronics can fail: buy local, from a tested brand with continuity.

13. Exchangeable

Suppliers should recommend options and help with layouts, but you may change your mind after installing, so choose one offering money-back or exchange.

14. How to position downlights

Place downlights about 3m apart, positioned by the room, not the furniture.

  • Never one central downlight. Small rooms: two, 600-700mm from the walls, over 900 lumens each.
  • Larger rooms: 4 in the corners about 650mm from each wall; 60º low glare lights suit these and central fans.
  • Kitchens: at least 3 wide-beam lights to limit shadows; add under-cabinet strip with low glare.
  • Passages and living areas: three metre spacing, aligned with other lights. Check beams before cutting holes; one light out of line looks bad.
  • Bathrooms: at least 2 downlights, or 1 with starlights, to cut mirror shadows.

15. Greenhse basic downlight easy selection

  • DL10ES: standard 10W tri-colour switch adjustable, wide beam.
  • DL10BT: 10W Bluetooth, wide beam, colour and brightness set on the phone.
  • DL10PS: 10W low glare tri-colour switch adjustable, 60° beam.
  • DL10PBT: 10W low glare Bluetooth, 60° beam, set on the phone.
  • DL9RGB: full-colour and colour temperature, wide beam, WiFi or Bluetooth.

WiFi costs less and needs no gateway for Alexa, Google or HomeKit, but needs a WiFi extender beyond 10 devices. Full-colour Bluetooth is more stable and easier to install but needs a gateway for those assistants.

16. How to choose downlight checklist

  • High lumens: 10Watt should achieve 940 lumens
  • Good dimming: at least 10%-100%; some reach 0% with specific dimmers
  • Colour switch: 3000k / 4000k / 5000k
  • Light colour: CRI of 80 or above
  • IC-4 or IC-F: essential
  • Certification and public liability: are you covered
  • Cords and plugs: installation, safety, replacement
  • High IP rating: IP65 and IP54 for wet areas or under eaves
  • Beam angle: suits the room
  • Low glare: comfort, or use with fans
  • Lifespan and warranty: at least 40 000 hours, 4 year warranty
  • Smart downlights: cheaper than adding dimmers
  • Exchangeable: if you change your mind

For help with LED downlights in Perth, visit Greenhse Technologies at 5/1 Locke Lane, Ellenbrook WA 6069 or phone (08) 9297 2969.
/blog/led-downlights-everything-you-need.bodyHtmlOriginal:
LED downlights have become the most common form of lighting in both homes and commercial installations. These can easily be sourced from numerous suppliers for under $10 and installation costs can be as low as $15 for replacing halogen lights, or between $20 and $35 for new installations. Builders can charge as high as $150 per fitting, and installed, so when installing downlights for a complete home, the savings can be high if you plan carefully.

In addition to the high cost, builders don’t always install the best or most appropriate options. They will often compromise the quality of the light to save a few dollars and do not offer selections that can change the lighting effect which can make your home ideal and set according to your preferences.

Good lighting in your home is an investment and therefore it is important to have a good understanding of all factors that should be considered.

This article will help you understand what choices are available, how to determine the quality of the fitting as well as tips for selecting and installing.

HOW TO COMPARE AND GET BETTER QUALITY DOWNLIGHTS:

1. LUMENS:

You are paying for light (Lumens), not Watts, so be careful not to select a downlight just by wattage. Although this is an indication, more efficient and better quality lights will have higher lumens/Watt that reduce your power usage. NB: Look for the output Lumens. Some suppliers and packaging will be misleading and will supply the LED chip lumens and not the actual output lumens. The output lumens will be about 15% less but sometimes even as much as half. If you are not sure from the packaging, do a comparison.

 

2. DIMMING:

Check that the downlights are dimmable. Most downlights are dimmable although the actual dimmer switch can affect the amount they dim. Some downlights do not dim as well as others and can also flicker on lower settings. Dimming can be very useful in creating the correct mood and reducing glare but, just as important, will save energy usage and often increase life span. When a downlight is dimmed, it saves power according to the level to which it is dimmed, unlike the old halogen globes that did not offer savings when dimmed.

 

3. LIGHT COLOUR:

The next critical selection is the Light Output Colour. Most downlights are now offered with a 3-colour switch, enabling you to select the light colour that suits you best. Cheaper downlights do not give you this option and if you are not happy with the colour chosen, you would need to purchase a new downlight. The 3 colours selected are also important: Warm White (3000k), Natural White (4000-4500k) and Cool White (5000-6000k) are the most common.

 

  • It is always important to check the Kelvin (k) value as some suppliers call 4000-4500k Cool White and 5000-6000k as Daylight or Bright White. This varies by manufacturer.

 

  • Warm White is soft and relaxing and is the preference of most hotels.
  • Natural White offers a cleaner light with less yellow; it is becoming the most common and popular choice in homes.
  • Cool White is preferred in a Work or Office environment. There has also been a trend to moving away from 6000k to 5000k, which is more comfortable on the eyes and has less harmful blue light yet is still bright and vibrant.
  • I would recommend purchasing an LED downlights that has a 3-colour switch with settings of 3000k, 4000k and 5000k. This should give you the best range and selection. 
  • There are also a variety of Smart Downlights that enable you to change and choose the exact colour temperature (k) between 2700k and 5700k, with dimming options that I will cover later.

 

4. CRI, LIGHT QUALITY:

Not all LED chips are the same. The Kelvin temperature given is an average value, so 2 different LED lights both on 3000k, 4000k or 5000k can look very different. It is hard to see this on the packaging so doing a comparison is a good idea. You can also compare the CRI value - CRI means the colour-rendering index. The higher the CRI, the better the light quality. Generally a CRI value over 80% is suitable for homes and >90 for shops and displays. I have seen some downlights with the same Kelvin which have unattractive green or pink tints. This will be unappealing in any home.

 

5. IC-4 or IC-F:

LED Downlights are generally safer than the old halogen fittings, however they do still get hot and need to be installed according to manufacturers’ specifications. All downlights should now have IC-4 or IC-F certification - IC-4 is a higher certification. This indicates less than a 0.4mm gap, preventing any ingress of insects or materials that could add to fire risk.

With this certification and built-in drivers, downlights can now be installed with abutting insulation, which means insulation gaps in your ceiling, or canisters, to prevent blow in are not required thus making your house safer and more efficient. Do not purchase downlights that do not have this certification and do not allow builders to install these as it compromises your ceiling and insulation efficiency, and more importantly, compromises your safety.

 

6. CERTIFICATION & PUBLIC LIABILITY:

Unlike IC-4 and IC-F certification which, although is extremely important, is not yet essential, downlights need to comply with Australian electrical wiring regulations to allow them to be installed. Numerous fittings claim to be certified but have wiring that does not meet Australian standards. The certification may be for part of the fitting only, done through a non-registered laboratory, or even worse not be genuine. If a fire is caused by a fitting which is found to not meet the required regulation requirements, or not be fitted by a registered electrician, you could lose everything, as insurers will not accept liability in these circumstances. Check the certification carefully and check that both the supplier and electrician being used have public liability insurance.

 

7. CORDS & PLUGS:

All downlights, unless in a concrete slab, come with cords and sockets. Electricians install plug bases in the ceiling, one for every downlight. Do not allow downlights to be hard-wired (installed without the sockets), unless in a slab, as this will void the IC-4/F certification, as well as make it more difficult and costly to replace your downlight if it fails or if you want to change it.

 

8. IP-RATING

The IP rating indicates how well the light is sealed. The higher the IP rating the better sealed it is. The first digit indicates the resistance to dust and particles, the second number indicates the resistance to water. For outdoor use for areas that get rain, IP65 is required.

For under eaves and wet areas IP54 is generally suitable (your electrician will check and verify requirements). 

A downlight that has a higher IP rating has the added advantage of preventing insects from getting into the fitting and affecting the appearance of the light.

 

9. BEAM ANGLE

Most downlights installed now have a flat white diffuser. This gives a good, wide spread of light, covering almost 180º in some cases. They are great for adding light to a room as they provide light that reaches the walls, making rooms look brighter. If the light in a room does not reach the walls, even if the lumens are very high, the room will still look dark. This makes the lights suitable for walk-in wardrobes, if spaced far apart, or if limited quantities are used, for example, two in a bedroom. There are also disadvantages, in that due to the wide spread of light, you get a lot of glare, which can be uncomfortable, especially if there are a lot of lights in an area. They are also not ideal if using in a room with a fan.

 

10. LOW GLARE

This has become an extremely overlooked option. With all the cheap, wide beam downlights on the market, combined with people experiencing disappointing results previously from old halogen lighting, most people are more concerned initially with supplying excessive bright. This takes away the relaxing feel and mood from a home and can produces an office-like effect. Recently Low glare lighting is making a come back, as people are now noticing the difference, and realising there are better options. These lights provide far less glare, are more comfortable, provide more mood and look nicer. The wide beam downlight is still preferable in some areas and lights can now be selected according to where and how they are being placed.

 

11. LIFESPAN & WARRANTY

Lifespan is an indication of how long the light will run for, indicated in hours. Most good quality downlights will have an expected lifespan of 40 000 hours. This is usually an indication of the number of hours the light will run before reaching 70% of its original brightness. The higher the lifespan is generally an indication of better quality LED chips. Some commercial LEDs can have lifespans of 120 000 hours. The downlight comprises of more than LED chips, it includes a driver and electronics as well. These can fail for a number of reasons before the projected lifespan of the LED chip.

Good quality lights will have a form of surge protection. Warranty periods can help give an indication of the reliability but with numerous small suppliers and online stores, warranties can far exceed the time businesses exist. Choose an established company, supplying brands from credible, listed Chinese companies. Not only does this ensure high quality levels, but also consistency and continuity of product, with supported warranties. Word of mouth and referrals can also assist, not only for good products and suppliers, but also indicating which ones to avoid. I see a number of brands being brought in to compare or swap and know of suppliers who have had over 50% failures within a 6-month period.

 

12. SMART DOWNLIGHTS

Downlights can be a very smart choice, not only can they be dimmed to save energy costs and achieve the desired mood, but also the colour temperature can be set and adjusted as required, not just to 1 of 3 settings, but anywhere from 2700k to 5700k. There are even full colour options now available. Smart lights can also include timers and alarms as well as being able to be connected to other smart devices. As with standard downlights, not all smart lights are the same and the following should be considered when purchasing.

 

  • Ensure the colour selection is good and can match your normal (non-Smart) downlights if required.
  • Ensure the dimming level is suitable and flicker-free.
  • Ensure the smart lights have permanent memory. Lights that can change colour with a switch will change your carefully selected settings and adjustments, cause different lights to change colours differently and cause a lot of wasted time and frustration.
  • Carefully select between WiFi and Bluetooth lights. Although WiFi lights can be good for certain applications, large quantities of WiFi lights can affect your WiFi bandwidth and its efficient functioning. Bluetooth downlights can achieve similar results with a cheap gateway added without the disadvantages, and offer other advantages, including easy set up and quick operation.
  • If selecting full colour (RGB) downlights, check the colour brightness, not just the white output, as these use different LED chips and lower colour output often results as it can save manufacturing costs.
  • Remember Smart lights will not function or be Smart if the light switch is off. To be completely Smart, changing the switch and light together will give full control. Smart, dimmable switches are not available yet, which could enable normal downlights to have Smart control, except these would still not have the colour temperature options.
  • There is more that can go wrong with a Smart light, due to added components and electronics. Follow the lifespan and warranty tips supplied above, and also try and purchase local, where you can get backup, support and easy replacements if unsuitable.
  • Ensure the brand has been tried and tested and will have continuity in the future.

 

13. EXCHANGEABLE

Lighting suppliers should know a lot more about downlights than you, should make recommendations, show you options and even assist with lighting layouts. At the end of the day however you still have your own personal preferences and may rather have your lighting selection over what is recommended. You may even change your mind after installing. Find a supplier that can be flexible, to reduce any risk of purchasing a product you find unsuitable, with money-back or exchange options. After all, the lights you choose should last a very long time, they could be the last lights that you change.

 

14. HOW TO POSITION: 

Downlights can now be placed about 3m apart. The idea behind downlights is to spread lights evenly throughout a home, and providing a good level of light to all areas. Downlights now look neat and blend with ceilings to give a good open feeling to enhance the size of homes and the layout. It is always best to position the downlights according to the rooms, rather than the furniture within a room, giving the best option to provide balanced lighting and flexibility.

  • Do not place 1 downlight in the centre of a room. The lumens are too low and light will not reach the walls. Two downlights about 600-700mm from the walls are normally suitable in small rooms, using downlights with over 900 lumens.
  • For larger rooms or if symmetry is preferred, 4 downlights are commonly used. Place in the corners about 650mm from each wall. Here 60º low glare downlights are far more suitable for comfort, and will also work well with a fan in the centre of the room if required.
  • In kitchens I would recommend more lights for the area than other rooms, normally at least 3 downlights to minimise shadows, and more for larger kitchens. The normal wide beam downlights are good and provide lighting over a larger area and into cupboard spaces. Low glare lights can also be used but supplementary lighting, such as strip lighting under cabinets, would help in combination with the downlights.
  • For passages and living areas, the density can be far less than previously with halogen lights. Three metre spacings are generally fine. Ensure lights in these areas work together with other downlights, creating a uniform and balanced layout in all directions. Mark and check that all lights can be installed prior to making any holes and ensure beams will not affect this. Lining up and spacing lights carefully will improve the aesthetics of your home, having even 1 light out of line can be extremely unattractive.
  • Bathrooms require at least 2 downlights, or 1 downlight in combination with starlights or another form of light. This will reduce shadows and make it easier to see in the mirror. 

 

15. GREENHSE BASIC DOWNLIGHT EASY SELECTION:

DL10ES: Standard 10W Tri-colour switch adjustable downlight; Wide beam angle

DL10BT: 10W Bluetooth downlight, wide beam angle - colour temperature and brightness are adjusted on the phone

DL10PS: 10W Low Glare Tri-colour switch adjustable downlight; 60° Beam angle

DL10PBT: 10W Low Glare Bluetooth Downlight; 60° Beam angle - Colour temperature and brightness are adjusted on the phone

DL9RGB: Full-Colour and colour temperature downlight with wide beam angle - is available in WiFi or Bluetooth.

WiFi has a lower cost and does not require a Gateway to work with Alexa, Google or Home Kit. These require a WiFi Extender when connecting more than 10 devices. 

Full-Colour Bluetooth is more stable and easier to install. However, it requires a Gateway to be operated with Alexa, Google or Home Kit. 

 

16. HOW TO CHOOSE DOWN-LIGHT CHECKLIST:

☑︎ High Lumens: 10Watt should achieve 940 Lumens

 

☑︎ Good Dimming: At least 10%-100%, some downlights with specific dimmers can also dim to 0%

 

☑︎ Colour Selecting Switch: e.g. 3000k / 4000k / 5000k 

 

☑︎ Good Light Colour: At least a CRI of 80 or above

 

☑︎ IC-4 or IC-F: Certification (essential, not an option)

 

☑︎ Certification & Public Liability: Does the supplier have you covered

 

☑︎ Cords & Plugs: For quick installation, safety and replacement

 

☑︎ High IP rating: For wet areas or under eaves, IP65 and IP54 options are available

 

☑︎ Beam angle: Does this suit the area and room

 

☑︎ Low glare:  Are you ensuring suitable comfort levels, or using with fans

 

☑︎ Lifespan & warranty: Ensure at least 40 000 hours, with 4 year Warranty 

 

☑︎ Smart downlights: Can be less expensive than adding dimmers, improving comfort and energy savings

 

☑︎ Exchangeable: Can you change your mind if the lights are not suitable

/blog/led-track-lighting-perth.html.bodyHtml:
Lighting plays a crucial role in the ambiance, functionality and energy efficiency of any space. Whether you are designing a cosy home interior or a modern office fit-out, choosing the right lighting solution makes a real difference to how the room looks and works. LED track lights have become a popular choice in Perth homes and businesses, and this post explains why, covering their versatility, energy savings, lifespan, colour options and the 15W and 30W fittings available from Greenhse Technologies.

Illuminate your space with LED track lights

A track lighting system is a length of powered rail, surface-mounted or suspended from the ceiling, with individual light heads that clip on anywhere along its length. Each head can be slid along the track, rotated and tilted, so the light can be aimed exactly where it is needed. Heads can be added, removed or repositioned later without any new wiring, which is what sets track lighting apart from fixed downlights or pendants.

Stylish and versatile lighting solution

LED track lights are known for their sleek, modern design that complements almost any interior. Their versatility makes them ideal for:

  • Highlighting artwork or displays: perfect for illuminating paintings, sculptures or retail merchandise, with the beam angled to lift the subject away from the wall.
  • Task lighting: focused light for kitchens, workspaces or conference rooms, where you need strong, even illumination on a bench or table.
  • Ambient lighting: heads aimed at walls or ceilings to create a warm, inviting atmosphere in living rooms or lobbies.

Because every head can be adjusted and directed independently, you have complete control over both the look and the function of the space. A single track can do several jobs at once, for example washing a feature wall at one end while lighting a dining table at the other. Explore the stylish range of LED track lights in Perth to find the right fit for your project.

Energy efficiency and cost savings

One of the most compelling reasons to choose LED track lights is their exceptional energy efficiency. Compared with halogen track heads, which were the standard for many years, LEDs consume far less electricity while delivering the same or better brightness. Halogen lamps convert most of their energy to heat rather than light, whereas an LED puts most of its power into visible light. That means lower energy bills, less heat load on air conditioning in a Perth summer, and a reduced carbon footprint, all important considerations for eco-conscious homeowners and businesses.

Durability and longevity

These LED fittings are built to last, with an average lifespan of up to 50,000 hours. At four hours a day, that is more than 30 years of use. Compared with traditional bulbs this means fewer replacements, less maintenance and greater peace of mind, which matters even more in commercial spaces with high ceilings where changing lamps requires ladders or lifts. Greenhse track lights are made with high-quality materials, including full aluminium housings that draw heat away from the LED chip, making them a reliable lighting solution for homes and offices in Perth.

Enhanced brightness and colour options

LED track lights offer high brightness levels and are available in a range of colour temperatures, from warm white through to cool daylight. Colour temperature is measured in kelvin (K) and describes how warm or cool the white light appears. This lets you tailor the lighting to the requirements of each space:

  • Warm light: ideal for creating a cosy atmosphere in living rooms, bedrooms and hospitality settings.
  • Cool light: perfect for workspaces, retail displays and areas that require focus and productivity.

A neutral white in between suits kitchens, galleries and general commercial areas where colours need to look natural. Explore the LED Track Lights range for powerful brightness that enhances your interiors effortlessly.

Perfect for homes and offices

Whether you are upgrading your home's lighting or improving productivity in an office, LED track lights provide the right balance of style, efficiency and functionality. They suit modern, functional architectural styles particularly well, and they are a practical choice for renovations because a single power point on the ceiling can feed a whole track of heads. Common applications include kitchen benches, home galleries, open-plan living areas, retail shops, cafes, showrooms and meeting rooms.

Affordable and accessible

With advances in technology, LED lighting is more affordable than ever. Greenhse Technologies offers high-quality LED track lights at competitive prices. Choose the LED Track Light 15W for smaller spaces and shorter throw distances, or the LED Track Light 30W for larger areas, higher ceilings and retail displays. Both can be mixed on the same track, so you can put higher output heads over a display and lower output heads over a walkway.

Planning a track installation

  • Decide what each head needs to light, then position the track so heads can be aimed at roughly 30 degrees to the surface to limit glare and reflections.
  • Choose the total number of heads so the track's power feed is not overloaded.
  • Select one colour temperature for the whole track for a consistent look.
  • Have the track and its power feed installed by a licensed electrician.

LED track lights are a versatile, energy-efficient and stylish lighting solution that can transform any home or office space in Perth. Their durability, adjustable brightness and modern design offer excellent value for money. Greenhse Technologies supplies a wide range of LED lighting products for residential, commercial and industrial use. To see the track lights in person, visit the LED Lighting Store at Unit 5, 1 Locke Lane, Ellenbrook WA 6069, or call (08) 9297 2969 for advice on the right fittings for your space.

/blog/lighting-layout-guidelines.html.bodyHtml:
Working out how many lights a room needs, and where to put them, is one of the most common questions we hear from Perth homeowners and electricians planning a new build or renovation. Too few downlights leave dark corners, too many waste money and create glare. This guide sets out the basic lighting layout guidelines Greenhse Technologies uses when marking up a floor plan, room by room, together with the compatible LED downlights and ceiling lights we recommend for each room size.

The two images below show the approach in practice: first a marked-up house plan with suggested light points, then a summary table of room sizes, layouts and recommended lights. The notes that follow explain how to read them and apply the same logic to your own plan.

Reading the floor plan

On the plan above, every dot is a suggested light point. Small rooms such as the larder, WC, walk-in robe and dressing room carry a single light in the centre of the ceiling. The kitchen has lights spaced along the bench run, the ensuite has a point over the vanity and another over the shower area, and the larger living, activity and master suite areas use a regular grid of four to eight points so the light overlaps evenly. The long green bar in the garage or alfresco area represents a linear fitting such as a batten or strip light rather than a downlight.

The principle is simple: light points are placed in a grid that matches the shape of the room, kept a consistent distance from the walls, and spaced so the beams overlap at working height. Furniture, benches and mirrors then decide where the grid shifts slightly so that task areas get direct light.

Room-by-room layout guide

Small rooms: up to 2m x 2m

Typical rooms are toilets, small bathrooms, ensuites, storage areas, walk-in robes, pantries and small patios. One light in the centre of the ceiling is enough. Recommended fittings are group 1 (DL10ES, DL10BT or DL9RGBW downlights) or group 3 (the P18S 18W ceiling light).

Medium rooms: 2m x 2m to 2.5m x 3.5m

Small bedrooms, bathrooms, ensuites, studies, passage areas, hallways, entrance ways, dressing rooms and patios fall into this bracket. Use two lights placed along the long axis of the room, each roughly a quarter of the way in from the short walls. Recommended fittings are again group 1 downlights or a group 3 ceiling light.

Large rooms: 2m x 2m to 4m x 4m

Bedrooms, studies, theatre rooms, ensuites, kitchens and alfrescos of this size suit a grid of four lights, one in each quarter of the ceiling. Recommended fittings are group 1 or group 2 downlights.

Larger rooms: 2m x 4m to 4m x 6m

Main bedrooms, kitchens, dining rooms, living areas and alfrescos of this size need a grid of six lights arranged in two rows of three. Recommended fittings are group 1 or group 2 downlights.

Long rooms: 2m x 5m to 4m x 8m

For long open-plan living and dining spaces, extend the grid to eight lights in two rows of four so that the spacing between points stays even from one end to the other. Recommended fittings are group 1 or group 2 downlights.

Rooms using ceiling lights: 2.5m x 5m to 3m x 6m

Where a surface-mounted oyster style light is preferred over downlights, a room of this size can be lit with two ceiling lights spaced along the long axis. Recommended fittings are group 3 (P18S) or group 4 (P24S).

Recommended compatible lights

  • Group 1: DL10ES, DL10BT and DL9RGBW. Suitable for smaller rooms up to 3.5m. The DL10ES is a 10W LED tri-colour downlight, the DL10BT is a 10W Bluetooth LED downlight, and the DL9RGBW is a 9W smart WiFi RGBW LED downlight for colour-changing scenes.
  • Group 2: DL10PS, DL10A gimbal, DL10GS and DL10PBT. The DL10PS is a 10W premium 60 degree beam LED downlight, the DL10PBT is its 10W premium Bluetooth 60 degree beam version, the DL10A is a 10W adjustable 60 degree LED downlight, and the DL10G is an IP65 rated 10W gimbal downlight. These narrower 60 degree beams are the better choice in larger rooms and under higher ceilings because they push light down where it is needed with less side spill and glare.
  • Group 3: P18S. An 18W LED ceiling light with 2-in-1 CCT, so the colour temperature can be selected at installation.
  • Group 4: P24S. A 24W LED ceiling light with 2-in-1 CCT, for the larger rooms in the last bracket.

Practical tips when planning your layout

  • Start with the room dimensions from your plan, match them to the closest size bracket above and mark the grid before you consider furniture.
  • Keep light points a consistent distance from the walls so the wash across the ceiling looks even from the doorway.
  • Over benches, vanities and desks, shift the nearest point so the beam lands on the work surface rather than behind your shoulder.
  • In bathrooms, ensuites and alfrescos choose fittings with a suitable IP rating for damp areas, such as the IP65 gimbal.
  • Tri-colour and CCT fittings let you settle on warm or cool white after the ceiling is finished, which avoids repainting decisions later.
  • All downlight and ceiling light installation and wiring must be carried out by a licensed electrician.

These layout guidelines are a starting point rather than a rule book, and every home has its own quirks in ceiling height, natural light and room use. /blog/low-glare-architectural-downlights.h1: Benefits of Low Glare/Architectural Downlights in Perth
/blog/low-glare-architectural-downlights.lede: Achieving brightly lit rooms is the primary focus for most homeowners.
/blog/low-glare-architectural-downlights.bodyHtml:
Achieving brightly lit rooms is the primary focus for most homeowners. However, there are several options that provide bright lighting and, more importantly, comfort, style and aesthetics. This post explains what glare is, how low-glare and architectural downlights reduce it, and how tri-colour and fully smart adjustable downlights let you fine-tune the light in every room.

LED downlights in Perth are the most popular new type of lighting. Placing downlights carefully in a home allows for even, bright lighting with very low running costs. The type of downlight you choose, though, makes a real difference to how comfortable the room feels.

The problem with regular downlights

Regular downlights have a PC (polycarbonate) diffuser that hides the LED chips. This gives a very wide spread of light, which is good for certain applications, but the whole face of the fitting glows and a lot of light shines sideways, directly into your eyes. The result is glare, which causes eye strain and discomfort, especially when you have 4, 6 or even 8 downlights in a room and several of them sit in your line of sight at once.

How low-glare downlights work

Low-glare downlights direct their light with a narrower beam angle, such as 60º, as opposed to the standard 100º to 120º. The LED sits deeper in the fitting behind a lens or reflector, so the light goes down onto the floor, benchtop or table rather than sideways into your eyes. From across the room you see a soft, dim ring rather than a bright disc.

Measuring glare: UGR

Glare on a downlight is measured in UGR, the Unified Glare Rating. The lower the UGR, the less glare. A UGR below 19 is the widely used benchmark for comfortable lighting in offices and living spaces, and a UGR below 16 is considered very low glare. In order to achieve a good balance between comfort and distributed lighting, a UGR of 19 or less is the target for most rooms, with slightly higher values acceptable in corridors and utility areas where nobody sits and looks up for long periods.

Architectural downlights

Architectural downlights in Perth incorporate low-glare lenses or deep reflectors to provide lighting without the discomfort of glare. Because the beam is more controlled, this lighting is also more direct, enabling certain areas and features to be highlighted, such as artwork, a kitchen island or a feature wall, thereby creating more ambience and mood. Many are available in black or white trims to match modern interiors.

Tri-colour downlights

Most downlights now come standard with a 3 colour selectable switch on the back of the fitting. This gives you the option of warm white (3000 Kelvin), natural white (4000K) and bright white or daylight (5000K). Some lights will also offer up to 6000K, although this is not recommended for homes because it looks blue and clinical.

As a guide, 3000K suits bedrooms and living rooms, 4000K suits kitchens, bathrooms and laundries, and 5000K suits garages, workshops and task areas. The switch is set once, usually by the electrician at installation, and the light stays at that colour temperature.

Fully smart adjustable downlights

A tri-colour light, once set, cannot be adjusted without getting back into the ceiling. Instead of that limitation, both standard and low-glare downlights can now be controlled with infinite colour temperature and brightness options, using smart devices such as Amazon Alexa, Google Home, a phone app or remotes.

It is easy to set a smart light to an exact colour temperature and brightness level that best suits the room and your preferences. The wall switch still turns the lights on and off as normal, and the light settings remain unchanged when the switch is used. To change a light, adjust it on a smart device, or with Alexa or Google, by simply saying "Alexa, turn lounge 20% warm white".

Smart downlights also make it possible to group lights, set schedules and create scenes, so a living room can run bright and cool during the day and warm and dim in the evening without touching a switch.

Choosing the right downlight for each room

  • Living rooms, bedrooms and dining areas: low-glare or architectural downlights, warm white, ideally dimmable or smart.
  • Kitchens and bathrooms: low-glare downlights over benches and vanities, natural white.
  • Hallways, garages and laundries: standard wide-beam downlights are acceptable, as glare matters less where people are passing through.
  • Feature areas: narrow-beam architectural downlights to highlight artwork or joinery.

Downlights must be installed by a licensed electrician, who can also set the tri-colour switch and confirm the fittings are compatible with any dimmer you choose.

Shop for designer LED downlights in Perth to enhance your home today. Greenhse Technologies stocks low-glare, tri-colour and fully smart adjustable downlights at the showroom at 5/1 Locke Lane, Ellenbrook WA 6069, and you can call (08) 9297 2969 for advice. You can also visit our online store, Greenhse Technologies, to explore our exclusive collection.

/blog/lumens-vs-watts-whats-the-differen.bodyHtml:
If you have ever stood in front of a lighting display trying to remember whether you need a "60W" bulb or an "800 lumen" one, you are not alone. For decades, people in Australia shopped for light bulbs by watts. Then LED lighting arrived and changed the system, but many people still buy lights the old way, without realising it costs them money and often gives the wrong brightness.

Here is a clear, no-nonsense breakdown of lumens vs watts: what each one actually measures, and how to use lumens to choose the right LED lighting for your home or business in Perth.

What are watts, really?

Watts measure power consumption, which is how much electricity a light fitting draws to run, not how bright it is. With old-style incandescent bulbs, watts and brightness were closely linked, because incandescent globes were so inefficient that most of the electricity they used was lost as heat rather than light. A 60W incandescent bulb was roughly the same brightness as any other 60W incandescent bulb, so shoppers naturally used wattage as a stand-in for brightness.

That shortcut worked while every bulb used the same outdated technology. It does not work anymore.

What are lumens?

Lumens measure light output, the actual amount of visible light a fitting produces. This number tells you how bright a light will be, regardless of the technology behind it or how much electricity it uses to get there.

The distinction matters enormously with LED lighting, because LEDs are dramatically more efficient than incandescent or halogen globes. An LED can produce the same brightness and the same lumen output using a fraction of the wattage. Two lights with very different wattages can be equally bright, and two lights with the same wattage can have wildly different brightness levels, depending on the technology.

In short: watts tell you the running cost, lumens tell you the brightness. If you shop for light based on watts alone, you could end up with a room that is far dimmer or far brighter than you expected.

Why the switch to LED changed everything

Before LEDs became mainstream, wattage was a decent, if imperfect, proxy for brightness because incandescent and halogen technology was fairly consistent. LED technology broke that link completely. Manufacturers can now produce a 9W LED downlight that puts out as much light as an old 60W incandescent bulb once did, using around 85% less energy in the process.

That is great news for power bills, but it means the old habit of "just buy the same wattage as before" no longer applies. If you replace a 60W incandescent bulb with a 60W-equivalent LED, you are not buying like-for-like brightness. Check the lumens, not the watts, to know what you are actually getting.

Rough watt-to-lumen equivalents

As a general guide, here is roughly how old incandescent wattage compares to the lumen output most people are used to:

  • 40W incandescent: about 400 to 450 lumens
  • 60W incandescent: about 750 to 850 lumens
  • 75W incandescent: about 1,000 to 1,100 lumens
  • 100W incandescent: about 1,500 to 1,600 lumens

When shopping for LED replacements, match the lumen figure on the packaging to these numbers rather than looking at the wattage. A 9W to 12W LED will typically deliver that 60W-equivalent brightness, and a 13W to 15W LED will get you into 100W-equivalent territory, at a fraction of the running cost.

How many lumens do you actually need?

Brightness needs vary by room and by task. As a rough starting point for Perth homes:

  • Living rooms: 1,500 to 3,000 lumens total, layered across ceiling lights and lamps
  • Kitchens: 3,000 to 4,000 lumens, since these are task-heavy spaces
  • Bedrooms: 1,000 to 2,000 lumens, with dimmable options for softer evening light
  • Bathrooms: 2,000 to 3,000 lumens, especially around mirrors and vanities
  • Home offices: 3,000 to 4,500 lumens to reduce eye strain during screen work
  • Outdoor areas and driveways: varies widely, but security and flood lighting often call for 2,000 lumens or more per fixture

These are general starting points. Room size, ceiling height, wall colour and how many fittings you use will all affect the ideal total. A dark-painted room with high ceilings needs more lumens than a small white room, and spreading the total across several fittings gives more even light than one very bright point.

Do not forget colour temperature

Lumens tell you how bright a light is, but colour temperature, measured in Kelvin, tells you what that light will look like. Warm white (around 3000K) suits bedrooms and living areas, neutral white (around 4000K) works well in kitchens and bathrooms, and cool white (5000K and above) is common in garages, workshops and commercial spaces. Many modern LED fittings, including CCT (colour-changing temperature) products, let you adjust this to suit the mood or task without swapping bulbs.

Shop smarter, not just cheaper

Once you compare lumens instead of watts, choosing the right LED lighting in Perth becomes far easier, and you avoid the common mistake of ending up with a room that is too dim or uncomfortably bright. Whether you are upgrading a single room or fitting out a whole home or commercial space, checking lumens first and wattage second is the easiest way to make sure your new lighting does what you need it to do.
